scenes.narration: Glucose enters and hexokinase traps it as glucose 6-phosphate, the true branch point of central metabolism. From here, the molecule faces a committed choice. Phosphoglucose isomerase channels it leftward into glycolysis, where the payoff is ATP and pyruvate, the energy currency the cell spends. Alternatively, glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase commits it rightward into the pentose phosphate pathway, whose products are NADPH for reductive biosynthesis and ribose 5-phosphate for nucleotide synthesis. The deciding factor is simple. What does the cell need right now? Energy or building blocks? This fork captures the entire logic of why the pentose phosphate pathway exists alongside glycolysis.

scenes.narration: NAD and NADP look almost identical, differing by a single phosphate, yet the cell keeps them in dramatically different states for dramatically different purposes. The NAD pool sits oxidized, roughly a thousand to one in favor of NAD⁺, because catabolism needs an electron acceptor ready to grab electrons from fuel. The NADP pool is the mirror image, held strongly toward NADPH, because anabolism and antioxidant defense need an electron donor on tap. Same backbone, opposite redox poise. By maintaining these as separate cytosolic pools, the cell can run breakdown and biosynthesis simultaneously without the two electron economies interfering with each other.
scenes.slideTitle: NAD versus NADP: Two Pools, Two Jobs
scenes.notes: NAD and NADP look almost identical, differing by a single phosphate, yet the cell keeps them in dramatically different states for dramatically different purposes. The NAD pool sits oxidized, roughly a thousand-to-one in favor of NAD-plus, because catabolism needs an electron acceptor ready to grab electrons from fuel. The NADP pool is the mirror image, held strongly toward NADPH, because anabolism and antioxidant defense need an electron donor on tap. Same backbone, opposite redox poise. By maintaining these as separate cytosolic pools, the cell can run breakdown and biosynthesis simultaneously without the two electron economies interfering with each other.

scenes.narration: Reactive oxygen species are molecules carrying super-energetic electrons that attack and damage proteins, lipids, and DNA. The cell's frontline defense is glutathione, which neutralizes these threats by taking the oxidative hit so other molecules don't have to. But once glutathione absorbs that hit, it becomes oxidized and useless, linked into the GSSG dimer. To get it back into the reduced protective GSH form, the cell spends NADPH. And where does that NADPH come from? The pentose phosphate pathway. So G6PD sits at the very root of antioxidant defense. Lose that enzyme, lose your ability to regenerate glutathione, and oxidative damage runs unchecked.

scenes.narration: The non-oxidative phase is best understood as carbon bookkeeping carried out by two enzymes, transketolase and transaldolase. Track the carbons. First, transketolase takes two five-carbon sugars and produces a three-carbon and a seven-carbon sugar. Then transaldolase converts that three plus seven into a six and a four-carbon sugar. Finally, transketolase acts again, turning a four and a five into a six and a three. Sum it all and the net result is clean. Three five-carbon sugars become two six-carbon sugars and one three-carbon sugar. That is how excess pentoses are recycled back into glycolytic intermediates when the cell needs energy more than ribose.

scenes.narration: The pentose phosphate pathway is not one fixed route, but four operating modes, and the cell selects among them based on what it needs. When it needs ribose for nucleotides but little NADPH, it runs only the non-oxidative phase. When it needs both NADPH and ribose in balance, it runs the oxidative phase straight through. When it needs lots of NADPH but little ribose, it routes ribose back into glycolytic intermediates and recycles them. And when it needs NADPH plus ATP, it pushes carbon all the way into pyruvate. One pathway, four behaviors, each a different combination of glycolysis, gluconeogenesis, and the shunt.
